claims.text: Enhanced thermodynamic integration using tailored collective variables can accurately determine melting temperatures for high-entropy alloys.
The proposed method can determine the enthalpy of fusion of high-entropy alloys.
The proposed method can determine the entropy of fusion of high-entropy alloys.
The proposed method can determine the volume change at melting of high-entropy alloys.
The proposed method is computationally efficient for high-entropy-alloy melting calculations.
Near-melting multi-component high-entropy-alloy solids possess inherent chemical disorder.
Collective variables can be designed to capture structural rearrangements occurring during melting.
Tailored collective variables capture local atomic rearrangements and solid-liquid phase coexistence at the interface.
Directing sampling along transition-relevant order parameters reduces the convergence time for free-energy differences.
Directed sampling minimizes errors associated with the large configurational space of high-entropy alloys.
Reduced convergence time and configurational-space errors yield improved estimates of melting properties.
Predicted melting temperatures will be within approximately 5–10% of experimental values.
The method will provide reliable estimates of fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting.
The method will significantly reduce computational effort relative to conventional calorimetric or first-principles approaches.
Standard finite-temperature first-principles calculations for high-entropy alloys face computational-feasibility constraints.
Traditional DSC measurements are experimentally intensive.
The approach is mainly applicable to high-entropy alloys with well-defined solid-liquid coexistence.
Accuracy may diminish for alloys with broad or diffuse phase boundaries.
Accuracy may diminish when the selected collective variables do not effectively describe melting.
Computational efficiency and error bounds depend on the choice and tuning of collective variables.
